highlights: Contemporary Alpine sanctuary with cinematic Dolomite views, serious spa rituals and mountain dining
description:
Aman Rosa Alpina brings the long-standing Rosa Alpina address into Aman’s orbit in San Cassiano, the polished Alta Badia village set beneath the crags of the UNESCO-listed Dolomites. The location is both quietly local and impressively connected: lifts and the wider Dolomiti Superski terrain are close in winter, while summer opens to flowered meadows, Ladin hamlets, mountain passes and hiking and biking routes below Lavarella and Conturines.

The renewed 51 rooms and suites translate Alpine materials into a more contemporary language, with timber, stone, generous windows and balconies framing the light and ridgelines outside. The mood is less chalet nostalgia than refined mountain calm, still grounded in a property whose hospitality lineage reaches back through the Pizzinini family’s long stewardship of this San Cassiano landmark.

Dining now moves across several distinct rooms. The Grill focuses on local ingredients through grilled meats, handmade pastas and antipasti, with a terrace for clear-weather views; Enju brings a refined Japanese hot-pot tasting experience to the mountains; Il Salotto shifts from coffee and small plates by day to cocktails by night, complemented by a discreet cigar lounge.

The Aman Spa gives the resort its most expansive new rhythm, spreading across two levels with seven private treatment suites, indoor and outdoor pools, hydrotherapy, an outdoor Jacuzzi, sauna and steam facilities, yoga studio, salon and a substantial fitness centre. After a day on skis or high trails, the spa’s forest outlook and mineral quiet deepen the sense of a Dolomite retreat reimagined for a sharper, more serene age.

highlights: Balinese village calm above the Ayung River Gorge, wrapped in rice-paddy greenery
description:
Amandari sits in Kedewatan, just outside Ubud, on the green lip of the Ayung River Gorge, with rice paddies, village paths and Balinese temple life forming part of its everyday setting. Ubud’s galleries, craft studios, royal palace and markets are close enough for cultural excursions, yet the resort feels removed from the centre’s traffic and noise.

Opened in 1989, the resort was conceived by Peter Müller as a traditional Balinese village rather than a conventional hotel. Stone gateways, thatched roofs, coconut and teak accents, garden courtyards and winding paths give the boutique-scale pavilions and villas a ceremonial rhythm, while the curved swimming pool echoes the terraced rice fields below. Some villas look directly across the Ayung valley, adding a more private, residential feel to the resort’s deeply local architecture.

The open-air Restaurant looks over the valley and serves Balinese, Indonesian and international dishes shaped by seasonal produce from the resort’s organic garden, local farms and daily seafood deliveries. The Terrace Bar sits beside the pool for light meals and cocktails, while the private Dining Balé occupies a dramatic perch on the gorge for intimate meals and Balinese feasts.

Wellness is woven into the landscape rather than separated from it: spa treatments, steam and sauna facilities, yoga, fitness, tennis and village walks sit alongside guided temple visits, rice-field trekking and cultural classes with the Kedewatan community. Balinese dance and music add a gentle daily connection to village life. The result is a luxury resort that feels unusually porous to its surroundings, preserving the intimacy and sacred texture of Ubud’s highlands.

highlights: Beach-fringed tented wilderness on Moyo Island, with whale sharks and untouched reefs
description:
Amanwana occupies a beach-fringed bay on Moyo Island, east of Bali, within Moyo Satonda National Park and beside the protected waters of the Flores Sea. Reached by air and boat through Sumbawa, it feels deliberately remote: jungle rises behind the camp, reefs begin close offshore, and the island’s waterfalls, forest trails and quiet beaches shape the sense of arrival.

The 17 luxury tents are set between shoreline and tropical foliage, each a permanent canvas hideaway of 58 square metres with either oceanfront, ocean-view or jungle outlooks. Interiors are restrained and comfortable rather than theatrical, with hardwood floors, large picture windows, Indonesian artwork, generous living areas and decks edged by coral stone. Full-board stays make the camp feel more like a small expedition base than a typical island resort.

The Restaurant looks across the Flores Sea towards Medang Island and the mountains of Sumbawa, serving fresh, unfussy cuisine with much of the produce grown or reared on the island. Beach picnics, private dining and sailing journeys extend the culinary mood into the landscape, while the spa sits as a wilderness hideaway amid turquoise water, reefs and forest.

Amanwana’s strongest character comes from its access to nature. The PADI Dive Centre supports scuba and snorkelling across protected reefs, and kayaks and paddleboards keep exploration close to the beach. Inland routes lead to waterfalls, limestone pools, bat caves and birdlife; offshore, Saleh Bay is known for year-round whale shark encounters. Rusa deer, macaques, wild boar, turtles, manta rays and reef fish contribute to a stay that is both luxuriously quiet and intensely alive.

highlights: Forest-wrapped Kyoto retreat where ryokan minimalism meets onsen rituals and garden stillness
description:
Aman Kyoto rests in Takagamine, Kyoto’s quiet northern district, in a secret garden at the foot of the Hidari Daimonji mountain. The setting feels secluded yet culturally precise: Kinkaku-ji, temple routes, craft traditions and many of Kyoto’s UNESCO-listed sites sit within easy reach, while Kyoto Station is about 30 minutes away by car.

The resort’s 26 guest rooms, suites and pavilions are arranged through forested glades and moss-lined paths, with a minimalist ryokan language shaped by timber, latticed screens, calm proportions and views into the trees. Rather than staging old Kyoto literally, the design distils it into shadow, grain, silence and careful thresholds, making the garden as important as the architecture. The low-density layout gives each building the feeling of a private viewing platform, particularly in seasons of maple, moss and snow.

Dining is anchored by Taka-An, where seasonal omakase and chef-led tasting menus explore Japanese culinary discipline in an intimate setting. The Living Pavilion offers Kyoto-inspired western and local cooking, afternoon tea and relaxed meals beside the garden, with terraces and fire-warmed interiors that shift gracefully between seasons.

Wellness centres on the mineral-rich hot springs feeding the Aman Spa’s private onsen rituals, complemented by treatments, movement and meditation. Tea ceremony, Zen practice, guided garden walks and seasonal cultural experiences deepen the resort’s connection to Kyoto without overwhelming its atmosphere of restraint. For a city associated with crowds and ceremonial splendour, Aman Kyoto’s rare distinction is its quietness: a forested urban sanctuary where the old capital is encountered through moss, water, craft and stillness.

highlights: Ago Bay onsen sanctuary of private thermal baths, sacred shrines and coastal forest
description:
Amanemu lies within Ise-Shima National Park on the forested edge of Ago Bay, a landscape of sheltered inlets, pearl rafts and sacred coastal culture in Mie Prefecture. The resort is positioned for a quieter reading of Japan: Ise Grand Shrine, Shinto traditions, ama diving heritage, island viewpoints and the Kumano Kodo pilgrimage routes all sit within the broader cultural geography of the stay.

The resort’s 24 suites and eight two-bedroom villas interpret the geometry of Japanese minka houses in a contemporary Aman key. Low-slung roofs, dark timber, broad terraces and deep eaves draw the eye towards garden or bay views, while every suite and villa has its own private onsen fed by mineral-rich hot spring water. The effect is residential, restrained and deeply tied to the rituals of bathing.

Dining follows the seasons of Ise-Shima. The restaurant looks across Ago Bay and works with local ingredients from the surrounding coast and countryside, while The Lounge beside the pool brings Japanese craft beers, regional fruit-and-herb cocktails and sunset views into the daily rhythm. Featured experiences range from shrine-inspired breakfasts to sake and tea tastings, giving the food programme a strong sense of place.

The wellness offering is central rather than supplementary: onsen-style bathing facilities, steam rooms, an outdoor pool, yoga studio, fitness centre and spa treatments make water and heat the property’s defining elements. Hiking, golf, shrine visits, boat excursions and encounters with pearl-diving culture extend the experience beyond the resort, but Amanemu’s signature remains the private thermal bath, the bay light and the unusually serene coastal silence.
